subject: Developing and testing functions to be used as reactives

messages.author: c8fe4075ec631c03
messages.subject: Developing and testing functions to be used as reactives
parts:
Hi,

  My workflow in R (studio) is to run commands in the console, or write them in the script and use the run command, until it approximates what I need, then make sure the whole script runs the task repeatedly.

  I can't yet see how to easily marry this with the ShinyServer() object and its reactives.

  If I have an existing server, what's the easiest way to test some functions - for example if reactive 'buildData' builds data and I want to prototype a new plot for it? or check the data is still sane?

  Ideally I should have some way to invoke a reactive, either with or without the web client operating, to produce it's data which I can then play with.

  I have some thoughts on how reactive functions might be mutated from their current state, by replacing the non-pure inline calls to reactive dependencies by formal function parameters - which could operate non reactively outside the server, but before I dive into that, I'd love to know how other people approach it.

-Alex

parts: Probably not efficient, but I normally run a reactivePrint on whatever function I'm testing, then have shiny display the output on a separate tabPanel (I keep one around for scratch work/checking until I'm done). Then I just look at the output to see if it's doing what I want, then tweak it until it does.

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Developing and testing functions to be used as reactives
parts: Thanks for your thoughtful questions and comments, Alex!

My workflow in R (studio) is to run commands in the console, or write them in the script and use the run command, until it approximates what I need, then make sure the whole script runs the task repeatedly.

My workflow in Shiny is similar except that instead of using the run command I reload the browser. Changes that are in ui.R and server.R should be reloaded automatically. If I can't tell from looking in the browser whether things are working, I use a combination of:
  • print() calls, and look in the console
  • Invoking browser() from somewhere, such as within a reactive
  • options(shiny.trace=TRUE) which shows the traffic going back and forth from the server
When I have a pretty sizable function to implement I often implement it in a clean script and then once it looks right integrate it into Shiny.

I can't yet see how to easily marry this with the ShinyServer() object and its reactives.

  If I have an existing server, what's the easiest way to test some functions - for example if reactive 'buildData' builds data and I want to prototype a new plot for it? or check the data is still sane?

You could do this:

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  ... reactive functions and whatnot ...
  buildData <- reactive(...)

  observer(function() {
    buildData()
    browser()
  })
})

I think from that browser prompt you should be able to see buildData and any other reactives and invoke them (though I haven't done it this way personally--I've just used browser to inspect local variables inside that function).
Ideally I should have some way to invoke a reactive, either with or without the web client operating, to produce it's data which I can then play with.

And probably essential for unit testing. The only problem I see with doing this without the web client (which is what we really want, right?) is that the input values need to come from somewhere, to prime everything. If you wouldn't mind providing the input values manually then this is a very tractable problem--in fact with the ::: operator you could probably get it to work today ;)

I have some thoughts on how reactive functions might be mutated from their current state, by replacing the non-pure inline calls to reactive dependencies by formal function parameters - which could operate non reactively outside the server, but before I dive into that, I'd love to know how other people approach it.

I can see the appeal of that approach for some cases, but it would really need a separate syntax from the reactive functions we have today. And I could see it being very confusing that you declare something that looks like a function and takes parameters, that you call as a function but DON'T (and can't) provide the parameters for.

Note that you can already get the benefits of this by simply writing a pure function and invoking it from a reactive:

# Pure function
buildDataImpl <- function(foo, bar, baz) {
  ...
}

shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  foo <- reactive(function() {...});

  buildData <- reactive(function() {
    buildDataImpl(foo(), input$bar, input$baz);  # dependencies taken here
  })
})

Obviously there is some boilerplate here, but hey, it's R, you can always abstract the boilerplate away with a clever enough function... :)
